products.name: Duolingo for Schools
products.note: AI: Adaptive assignments. Who: Students, teachers. Student age: Under-13 users allowed with restrictions: no public profile, leaderboards, forums, or social logins; non-personalized ads under 16. Privacy: No signed California Student Data Privacy Agreement per a K-12 data leadership directory. Price: Duolingo for Schools is free.

reading.body:
Duolingo's only tracked AI product is a free school tool, and the record shows no signed California student data privacy agreement for it.

The pattern here is a consumer language company whose AI footprint in this data is a single education product, Duolingo for Schools, offering adaptive assignments to students and teachers at no cost. The restrictions on under-13 accounts are about social surface, not about the AI: no public profile, leaderboards, forums, or social logins, and non-personalized ads under 16. The privacy gap is the one concrete finding, a K-12 directory noting no signed California Student Data Privacy Agreement.

For AI specifically, this is a deployment question rather than a compute question. Adaptive assignment generation is inference at classroom scale, which is small relative to training, and nothing in this data speaks to where that inference runs, what it costs, or what hardware serves it. The absence of a signed state privacy agreement matters because schools are a procurement channel where paperwork gates adoption, and a free product still has to clear it.

What this does not tell the reader is how much of Duolingo's product is actually AI-driven, how many students use the school offering, or whether the missing agreement reflects a refusal, an oversight, or a directory that simply has not been updated. It also carries no energy, data center, or grid information, so it cannot support any claim about AI's physical constraints.

profile_text.body:
Duolingo is a public company, listed on SEC EDGAR as registrant Duolingo, Inc. under CIK 0001562088 and trading as DUOL. Its website describes it as a way to learn languages by playing a game, saying it is 100% free, fun, and scientifically proven to work, and calling itself the world's most popular way to learn a language, available on duolingo.com and on its apps.

The site's product material covers Duolingo for Schools, listed under education and research AI, which the company describes as offering adaptive assignments for students and teachers. It is free. The site states that under-13 users are allowed with restrictions: no public profile, leaderboards, forums, or social logins, and non-personalized ads under 16. It also states there is no signed California Student Data Privacy Agreement per a K-12 data leadership directory.

No lawsuits or MCP servers are recorded for the company.
